intro.title: Your first program
intro.bodyMarkdown:
Python is a programming language: a way to write instructions a computer can follow. It reads almost like English, which makes it a popular first language, and it's used everywhere, from websites and games to data analysis, science and AI.

A Python program is a list of instructions that run from top to bottom, one line at a time. In CodeQuest you type code into the sandbox or a challenge, press **Run** or **Check**, and Python runs right here in your browser.

Your first instruction is `print()`. Whatever you put inside the brackets is shown as output. Text goes in quotes, so Python knows it is text and not code. Numbers and maths don't need quotes.

```
print("Hello, world!")
print(42)
print(2 + 3)
```

Each `print()` writes one line. The quotes make all the difference: `print("2 + 3")` shows the text `2 + 3`, while `print(2 + 3)` works out the sum and shows `5`. You can also give `print` several things separated by commas, and it shows them with a space between: `print("2 + 3 =", 2 + 3)` shows `2 + 3 = 5`.

Lines that start with `#` are **comments**. Python skips them; they are notes for the people who read the code. A comment can also go at the end of a line.

```
# Say hello
print("Hi!")  # this line prints Hi!
```

Mistakes are normal, and Python tells you about them. When it can't run your code, it stops and shows an **error message**. Read the last line first. `SyntaxError` means the code isn't written correctly, such as a missing bracket or quote. `NameError: name 'pritn' is not defined` means Python doesn't know a name, usually because of a typo.

Python is case-sensitive: `print` works, `Print` doesn't. Spelling matters exactly in the text you print too, because the challenges compare your output character by character.

intro.title: Printing output
intro.bodyMarkdown:
`print()` is how your program talks to you, and it has a few options worth knowing. Give it several values separated by commas and it prints them on one line, with a space between each: `print("Score:", 42)` shows `Score: 42`. That's an easy way to mix text and numbers.

`sep` changes what goes **between** the values, and `end` changes what comes **after** the last one, which is normally a new line. With `end=""` the next `print` carries on the same line.

```
print("a", "b", "c", sep="-")   # a-b-c
print("Loading", end="")
print("...")                    # Loading...
```

Inside text, a backslash starts an **escape sequence**: `\n` is a new line and `\t` is a tab, which jumps to the next column. So a single `print` can show several lines: `print("Line 1\nLine 2")`. To print a backslash itself, write two: `\\`.

Text can be written with double quotes `"..."` or single quotes `'...'`. To show one kind of quote, wrap the text in the other kind: `print('She said "hi"')` and `print("It's sunny")`. You can also escape a quote with a backslash: `print("She said \"hi\"")`.

`print()` with nothing inside prints an empty line, which is handy for spacing out output. For text over several lines, triple quotes keep the line breaks exactly as you type them:

```
print("""Shopping list:
- apples
- bread""")
```

`print` shows values as plain text: `print("hi")` shows `hi` without quotes. When you need to see exactly what a value is, `repr()` shows it the way you'd write it in code: `print(repr("hi"))` shows `'hi'`, quotes included. That makes stray spaces easy to spot, because `repr(" hi ")` is `' hi '`.

intro.title: Variables
intro.bodyMarkdown:
A **variable** is a name for a value. You create one with `=`: `age = 30` means "let the name `age` refer to 30". After that, you can use the name wherever you'd use the value, and Python looks the value up.

```
age = 30
name = "Ana"
print(name, "is", age)   # Ana is 30
```

`=` means "assign", not "equals". Python works out the right side first and then stores the result under the name on the left. That's why `count = count + 1` makes sense: take the current count, add 1, and store the result back in `count`. Using a name before you've assigned it gives a `NameError`.

A variable can be reassigned at any time: the new value simply replaces the old one. It can even switch to a different kind of value, although that tends to confuse readers.

**Naming rules.** Names can contain letters, digits and underscores, but they can't start with a digit (`2fast` is not allowed), can't contain spaces or dashes (`total-score` would mean "total minus score"), and can't be one of Python's keywords, such as `class` or `if`. Names are case-sensitive: `score` and `Score` are two different variables.

Python's style guide, PEP 8, recommends `snake_case`: lowercase words joined by underscores, like `total_price`. Choose names for what a value means. `seconds_per_day = 86400` explains itself; `x = 86400` doesn't.

There are shortcuts for assigning several names at once. `x, y = 10, 20` gives `x` the value 10 and `y` the value 20, and `a = b = 0` sets both to 0. To swap two values, write `a, b = b, a`: the right side is worked out completely before anything is stored.

```
x, y = 10, 20
x, y = y, x
print(x, y)   # 20 10
```

Variables let you write a calculation once and reuse it. Change a value at the top of the program, and every line that uses it follows.

intro.title: Data types
intro.bodyMarkdown:
Every value in Python has a **type**, and the type decides what you can do with it. The basic types are `int` for whole numbers (42, -7), `float` for numbers with a decimal point (3.14), `str` for text in quotes, `bool` for `True` and `False`, and the special value `None`, which means "no value".

```
print(type(42))      # <class 'int'>
print(type(3.14))    # <class 'float'>
print(type("hi"))    # <class 'str'>
print(type(True))    # <class 'bool'>
print(type(None))    # <class 'NoneType'>
```

`type(value)` tells you a value's type. Quotes change everything: `42` is an int, but `"42"` is a str, text that happens to contain digits. And `3.0` is a float even though it's a whole number, because of the decimal point.

The type decides what operators do. `+` adds numbers but joins text: `2 + 3` is `5`, while `"2" + "3"` is `"23"`. Mixing text and a number, as in `"Age: " + 30`, raises a `TypeError`, because Python won't guess whether you meant maths or text. (A later lesson shows how to convert between types.)

Ints and floats mix freely, and the result is a float: `2 + 0.5` is `2.5`. Dividing with `/` always gives a float, even `10 / 2`, which is `5.0`.

`bool` values often come from comparisons: `5 > 3` is `True` and `2 == 3` is `False` (`==` asks "is it equal?"). The Decisions and loops section uses them to make decisions. Note the capital letters: it's `True` and `False`, never `true`.

`None` stands for "nothing here (yet)", such as a result you don't have. It isn't 0 and it isn't empty text; it's its own value with its own type.

To check whether a value has a certain type, use `isinstance(value, int)`, which returns `True` or `False`. One surprise: `bool` is a kind of `int` in Python, so `isinstance(True, int)` is `True`, and `True + True` is `2`. That's handy for counting how many things are true.

intro.title: Numbers and arithmetic
intro.bodyMarkdown:
Python makes a great calculator. `+`, `-`, `*` and `/` work as you'd expect, and `**` raises a number to a power: `2 ** 10` is `1024`.

Division comes in three flavours. `/` gives the exact result as a float: `7 / 2` is `3.5`. `//` is **floor division**: it divides and drops the fraction, so `7 // 2` is `3`. `%` (**modulo**) gives the remainder: `7 % 2` is `1`. Together, `//` and `%` split something into whole groups and leftovers:

```
minutes = 135
print(minutes // 60, "hours and", minutes % 60, "minutes")   # 2 hours and 15 minutes
```

`%` is useful beyond leftovers: `n % 2` is 0 for even numbers and 1 for odd ones, and `n % 10` is the last digit of `n`. Likewise, `n // 10` drops the last digit.

Python follows the usual order of operations: `**` first, then `*`, `/`, `//` and `%`, and finally `+` and `-`. So `2 + 3 * 4` is `14`. Use brackets to choose your own order: `(2 + 3) * 4` is `20`. When in doubt, add brackets; they make the code clearer, too.

Updating a variable with arithmetic is so common that it has shortcuts: `score += 10` means `score = score + 10`. There are also `-=`, `*=`, `/=` and `//=`.

```
score = 0
score += 10
score *= 3
print(score)   # 30
```

Two details. `//` always rounds **down**, so `-7 // 2` is `-4`, not `-3`. And ints can be as big as you like: `2 ** 100` is worked out exactly. Write big numbers with underscores to make them readable: `1_000_000` is the same as `1000000`.

intro.title: Math functions
intro.bodyMarkdown:
Python has built-in functions for everyday maths. `abs(-7)` is the distance from zero, `7`. `min(3, 9, 4)` and `max(3, 9, 4)` give the smallest and the largest of their values, here `3` and `9`. `pow(2, 5)` is the same as `2 ** 5`.

`round(x)` rounds to the nearest whole number, and `round(x, 2)` to 2 decimal places: `round(3.14159, 2)` is `3.14`. One surprise: exact halves round to the nearest **even** number, so `round(2.5)` is `2` but `round(3.5)` is `4`. This "banker's rounding" stops totals from always drifting upwards.

`divmod(a, b)` gives you `a // b` and `a % b` at once, as a pair you can unpack into two names: `hours, minutes = divmod(135, 60)` sets `hours` to 2 and `minutes` to 15.

For more maths, **import** the `math` module: write `import math` at the top of your program, then use its functions with a dot. `math.sqrt(25)` is the square root, `5.0`. `math.pi` is π. `math.floor(3.7)` rounds down to `3` and `math.ceil(3.2)` rounds up to `4`.

```
import math

print(math.sqrt(16), math.pi)            # 4.0 3.141592653589793
print(math.floor(3.7), math.ceil(3.2))   # 3 4
```

**Floats aren't exact.** A float is stored in binary, so most decimals are kept as a tiny bit more or less than what you typed. That's why `0.1 + 0.2` prints `0.30000000000000004`. It isn't a Python bug; every programming language does this.

So don't compare floats with `==`. Round both sides first, or use `math.isclose(a, b)`, which is `True` when two numbers are equal apart from such tiny errors. For money, a common trick is to count in cents, using ints.

To sum up the ways of dropping a fraction: `round` goes to the nearest whole number, `math.floor` always goes down (so `math.floor(-3.7)` is `-4`), and `math.ceil` always goes up.

print(0.1 + 0.2, math.isclose(0.1 + 0.2, 0.3))

intro.title: Strings
intro.bodyMarkdown:
A **string** (`str`) is a piece of text: a sequence of characters in quotes. You've printed plenty of them; now let's work with them. `+` joins strings and `*` repeats them: `"Py" + "thon"` is `"Python"` and `"ha" * 3` is `"hahaha"`.

`len(text)` counts the characters, spaces included: `len("hi there")` is `8`. The empty string `""` has length 0.

Each character has a position, its **index**, and counting starts at **0**: `word[0]` is the first character and `word[1]` the second. Negative indexes count from the end, so `word[-1]` is the last character. An index past the end raises an `IndexError`.

```
word = "Python"
print(word[0], word[1], word[-1])   # P y n
print(len(word))                    # 6
```

A **slice** takes a part of a string: `word[start:end]` runs from `start` up to, but not including, `end`. Leave out a side to go to the edge: `word[:3]` is the first three characters (`"Pyt"`), `word[3:]` is everything from index 3 (`"hon"`), and `word[-3:]` is the last three.

```
word = "Python"
print(word[0:2], word[:3], word[3:], word[-3:])   # Py Pyt hon hon
```

`in` checks whether one string appears inside another: `"cat" in "concatenate"` is `True`. Like everything about strings, it's case-sensitive: `"A" == "a"` is `False`.

Strings are **immutable**: you can't change a character in place, so `word[0] = "J"` raises a `TypeError`. Instead, build a new string, such as `"J" + word[1:]`, and assign it to a name.

To join a string and a number with `+`, turn the number into text first with `str()`: `"Age: " + str(30)`. The next two lessons show neater ways: string methods and f-strings.

intro.title: String methods
intro.bodyMarkdown:
Strings come with **methods**: functions you call on a string with a dot, like `text.upper()`. A method never changes the original string (strings are immutable). It returns a new one, so store the result: `name = name.strip()`.

**Changing case.** `upper()` and `lower()` turn every letter into a capital or a small letter, and `title()` capitalises the first letter of each word. `lower()` is handy for comparing text without caring about case: `answer.lower() == "yes"` is true for `Yes`, `YES` and `yes`.

**Cleaning up.** `strip()` removes spaces (and new lines) from both ends, while `lstrip()` and `rstrip()` only do the left or the right end. `replace(old, new)` swaps every `old` for `new`: `"2026/10/16".replace("/", "-")` is `"2026-10-16"`.

Methods can be **chained**: each one works on the result of the one before. `name.strip().title()` first strips the spaces, then title-cases what's left.

```
name = "  ada LOVELACE "
print(name.strip().title())   # Ada Lovelace
```

**Searching.** `count(sub)` counts how often `sub` appears. `find(sub)` gives the index where it first appears, or `-1` if it isn't there. `startswith(prefix)` and `endswith(suffix)` return `True` or `False`: `"photo.jpg".endswith(".jpg")` is `True`.

**Checking content.** `isdigit()` is `True` when every character is a digit, as in `"2026".isdigit()`, and `isalpha()` when every character is a letter. They're useful before turning input into a number.

**Splitting and joining.** `split()` breaks a string into a list of words at the spaces, and `split(",")` breaks it at the commas. `", ".join(words)` glues a list of strings back together, with `", "` between the pieces. (Lists get their own section later; for now, think of them as the pieces in square brackets.)

```
words = "red green blue".split()
print(words)              # ['red', 'green', 'blue']
print(" + ".join(words))  # red + green + blue
```

intro.title: f-strings and formatting
intro.bodyMarkdown:
Building text out of pieces with `+` and `str()` gets messy quickly. An **f-string** is much neater: put an `f` in front of the opening quote, and write any variable or expression inside `{curly braces}`. Python replaces each one with its value.

```
name = "Ana"
age = 30
print(f"{name} is {age} years old.")   # Ana is 30 years old.
print(f"Next year: {age + 1}")          # Next year: 31
```

Anything that gives a value can go inside the braces: maths, method calls, indexes, as in `f"{name.upper()} has {len(name)} letters"`. Without the `f`, the braces are just printed as they are.

After the value, a colon starts a **format spec** that controls how the value looks. `:.2f` shows a number with exactly 2 decimals, which is perfect for money: `f"{4.5:.2f}"` is `4.50`. `:,` adds thousands separators: `f"{1234567:,}"` is `1,234,567`. They can be combined: `f"{1234.5:,.2f}"` is `1,234.50`.

`:%` shows a fraction as a percentage, so `f"{0.256:.1%}"` is `25.6%`.

A number after the colon sets a **width**: the value is padded with spaces to that many characters, which lines up columns. `<`, `>` and `^` align the value to the left, right or centre. Inside an f-string, write text values with the other kind of quote, as in `{'Item':<8}`:

```
print(f"{'Item':<8}{'Price':>8}")
print(f"{'Tea':<8}{2.5:>8.2f}")
print(f"{'Cake':<8}{12:>8.2f}")
```

Writing `{value=}` shows both the expression and its value, a quick way to check what your variables hold: `f"{age=}"` gives `age=30`. To show a real curly brace, double it: `f"{{x}}"` prints `{x}`.

intro.title: Converting types
intro.bodyMarkdown:
Often a value has the wrong type for the job: text that holds a number, or a number you want to put into text. Each type's name works as a converter: `int()`, `float()`, `str()` and `bool()`.

```
print(int("42") + 1)       # 43
print(float("2.5") * 2)    # 5.0
print("Age: " + str(30))   # Age: 30
```

`int()` on a float **cuts off** the fraction; it doesn't round. `int(3.9)` is `3`, and `int(-3.9)` is `-3`. Use `round()` when you want the nearest whole number.

Turning text into a number only works when the text looks like that number. `int("42")` works, and so does `int(" 42 ")`, because spaces around the digits are ignored. But `int("4.5")`, `int("42 kg")` and `int("")` all raise a `ValueError`. `float("4.5")` works, and to get an int from `"4.5"`, go through float first: `int(float("4.5"))`.

`int()` can also read numbers written in other bases, if you tell it which: `int("ff", 16)` is `255` (hexadecimal, as in colour codes) and `int("101", 2)` is `5` (binary).

`bool()` follows Python's idea of **truthiness**. Zero and "empty" values are falsy: `0`, `0.0`, `""` and `None` all give `False`. Everything else is truthy and gives `True`, including the texts `"0"` and `"False"`, because they aren't empty.

```
print(bool(0), bool(""), bool(None))   # False False False
print(bool(7), bool("0"), bool(" "))   # True True True
```

intro.title: Reading input
intro.bodyMarkdown:
Programs get more interesting when they react to the person using them. `input()` pauses the program, waits for the user to type a line, and returns what they typed. Put a question inside the brackets and it's shown first, as a **prompt**:

```
name = input("What's your name? ")
print(f"Nice to meet you, {name}!")
```

**In CodeQuest,** type the answers into the sandbox's **Input** box before you press Run, one line for each `input()` call. Python reads them in order. If the program asks more questions than there are lines, you get an error saying `input()` needs a value. (Try the sandbox below: type `Ana` and `30` on two lines.)

`input()` **always returns a string**, even when the user types digits, so `input("Age? ") + 1` raises a `TypeError`. Convert the answer first: `age = int(input("Age? "))`, or use `float(...)` for decimals.

People type messily, with extra spaces and random capitals. `.strip()` removes the spaces at the ends, and `.lower()` lets you compare without caring about case: `answer = input("Continue? ").strip().lower()` turns `" Yes "` into `"yes"`.

If the user types something that isn't a number, `int()` raises a `ValueError` and the program stops. For now, assume the input is right; in the Errors and exceptions section you'll learn to catch the mistake and ask again.

A typical small program has three parts: **read** the input, **process** it (convert and calculate), and **print** the result. Keeping the parts apart, with a clear name for each value, makes the program easy to follow:

```
km = float(input("Distance in km: "))
miles = km * 0.621371
print(f"{km} km is {miles:.2f} miles")
```

The prompt is printed without a new line, so the user's answer appears right after it. End your prompts with a space (or a `\n` if the answer should go on the next line).

age = int(input("How old are you? "))
